label: explain2-leanbio-enhancers
one_line: We test whether a DNA switch has one fixed strength or a strength that changes with its partner, and how to tell that apart from chance.
what: Cells have DNA switches called enhancers. DNA is the long molecule that stores a cell's instructions. An enhancer turns up a gene, which is one recipe in that book. It does this through a second switch next to the gene, called a promoter. We ask a simple question. Line up enhancers from weakest to strongest on one promoter. Is the line-up the same on another promoter? If yes, each enhancer has just one strength. If no, strength depends on the pairing. We reread a public set of mouse measurements. It covers 98 enhancers on 15 promoters. We also ran a computer simulation of pure chance. And we wrote a proof that a computer checked, line by line, about what simple models allow.
why: Doctors and engineers want to design DNA switches that work in a chosen gene. That is easier if an enhancer has one fixed strength. It is harder if strength depends on the partner. Past studies disagree. So a clear test helps. We do not claim a final answer here. We claim only a sharper way to ask the question.

steps.text: We read the main papers on this question. A large human study found a simple pattern. In it, each enhancer has one strength, and each promoter scales that strength up or down by a fixed amount. Fruit fly and mouse studies found pickier pairings.
steps.picture: Reading three reviews of the same restaurant before you eat there.

steps.text: We took a public set of measurements from mouse cells. It has 98 enhancers. Each was measured on 15 promoters. Every measurement was done 3 times.
steps.picture: Timing 98 runners on 15 different tracks, three times each.

steps.text: For each pair of promoters we asked how well the two line-ups of enhancers agree. We used a score called the Spearman score. It runs from -1 to 1. A score of 1 means the same order. A score of 0 means no link. Our middle score was 0.382. That is a weak link.
steps.picture: Comparing two teachers' grade lists for the same class. Most students move up or down the list.

steps.text: We counted pairs of enhancers whose order flips between promoters. We only counted pairs where the gap was large enough to trust on both promoters. Then we compared the count with what measurement noise alone would give. Noise is the small random error that makes repeat measurements differ.
steps.picture: Checking if a coin that landed heads 60 times in 100 is really unfair.

steps.text: We fitted the simplest pattern. Each enhancer gets one strength, and each promoter multiplies it by a fixed number. Then we measured how much of the data was left unexplained.
steps.picture: Laying a straight ruler along a curved line and measuring the gap.

steps.text: We ran a computer simulation with no real pairing effect at all. It shows how often noise alone swaps the order of two enhancers. We call this the chance baseline.
steps.picture: Shuffling a deck many times to see what luck looks like.

steps.text: We wrote a proof about simple models and had a computer check each step. The proof is about a ceiling, a top level that output cannot pass. A ceiling squashes strong enhancers to the same top level. Squashed enhancers end up equal. Equal is a tie. A ceiling cannot make a weaker one beat a stronger one. So a ceiling makes ties but never swaps.
steps.picture: A speed limit can make two cars tie at 65 miles an hour. It never makes the slower car win.

steps.text: We also proved what a flip does not tell you. Several different causes could give the same flip.
steps.picture: A wet street can mean rain, a hose or a passing truck.

steps.text: We suggest one extra experiment. Turn each enhancer up in steps, from weak to strong. Do this on two very different promoters. Repeat every measurement three times. If the enhancers only tie at the top, a ceiling is the cause. If they truly swap, the pairing is the cause.
steps.picture: Turning a volume knob in steps on two different speakers, to see if both just max out or if one really sounds different.

wrong_if: Our bet, written down before we looked, is this. In real data, enhancer order flips between promoters more often than noise alone predicts. If flips were no more common than that chance baseline, we are wrong. Then one fixed strength per enhancer would be enough.
could_go_wrong: The 98 enhancers are DNA stretches that look like switches. Nobody tested each one on its own.
We had only 3 repeats per measurement. So our estimate of noise is rough.
Our chance simulation assumes tidy, even noise. Real counts are messier, especially for weak enhancers.
We could not read the large human data set. So we did not rerun that analysis ourselves.
Two of the sources are early drafts. Other scientists have not yet reviewed them. We read only their summaries.
The extra experiment we suggest is a prediction from a simulation. It is not a result from a lab.
We have not compared the real flip counts with the range from our own chance simulation. That final step is still undone.
Studies disagree, and their different designs may explain some of the gap.

questions.a: We reran public data and got the numbers in the check list below. A second set of checkers confirmed most of the key claims. Some were only partly confirmed, and we say so.

We did not rerun the large human data set. We did not test each enhancer in a lab. We did not compare real flip counts with the range from our own chance simulation. We do not know how big the effect is in most human cells.

questions.q: Is the answer yes or no?
questions.a: We do not know. The mouse data show real pairing effects. The big human study found a mostly simple pattern. Both can be partly true.
Take two enhancers, A and B. On one promoter A is stronger. On another promoter B is stronger. That swap of places is a flip.

questions.q: How big is the pairing effect in the mouse data?
questions.a: Think of all the ups and downs in the 98 by 15 table. The one-strength pattern explains about 71 out of every 100 parts of them. The part it misses is the pairing effect. That leftover is about 12 times bigger than the leftover we would expect from measurement noise alone. So the leftover is far too big to be just noise.

questions.q: Do the real flips beat chance?
questions.a: In the mouse table, 65,174 of 224,658 clear-cut pairs flipped. That is about 29 out of every 100. A simple noise model in the same analysis expected only about 368 flips, which is far fewer. But our separate chance simulation gives a wide range, and we have not yet set the real rate against that range. So we call this a strong hint, not a final answer.

questions.q: Why is the chance range so wide, 1.3 to 43.7 percent?
questions.a: Noise matters more when enhancers are close in strength. If enhancers are far apart, noise rarely swaps them. If they are bunched together, noise swaps many. Fewer repeats also mean more noise. Our simulation tried many settings of noise, repeats and spread. At the calm end, 1.3 in 100 pairs swapped. At the noisy end, 43.7 in 100 swapped. So a raw count of flips proves little until you match it to the noise level.

A flip rules out the simple models we proved things about. Those models say each enhancer has one strength and a ceiling. A flip does not say which other cause is true. Several different causes give the same flip.

questions.q: Why does a ceiling make ties but not swaps?
questions.a: A ceiling squashes strong enhancers to the same top level. Two squashed enhancers become equal, which is a tie. The ceiling treats a stronger enhancer at least as well as a weaker one. So it can never put the weaker one ahead.

Test each enhancer at several strengths on two very different promoters, with three repeats. If enhancers only tie at the top, that points to a ceiling. If they really swap places, that points to a true mismatch. We do not yet know which one the real data show.

glossary.plain: A stretch of DNA that turns a gene up.
The start switch of a gene, where reading of the gene begins.
The long molecule in cells that stores the instructions for life.
A stretch of DNA that holds the recipe for one product the cell makes.
Random error that makes repeated measurements differ a little.
Measuring the same thing again to see how much the result moves.
The line-up of items from weakest to strongest.
Each enhancer has one strength. Each promoter multiplies it by its own fixed number, like a volume dial that is the same for every enhancer.
A top level that the output cannot go above, however hard you push. Like a cup that is full: pouring more in changes nothing.
A result that depends on which enhancer is paired with which promoter.
What you would see if only random noise were at work.
A computer run that imitates a process using random numbers.
A computer program that checks each step of a maths proof. The one we used is called Lean.
A simple rule that tries to explain data.
A number from -1 to 1 that says how closely two line-ups match. 1 means the same order. 0 means no link. We used the Spearman score.
A collection of measurements shared for others to use.
Two enhancers swap which one is stronger when moved to another promoter.
Two enhancers whose gap in strength is big enough to trust on both promoters.
Parts out of every 100.
A paper shared before other scientists have reviewed it. Our drafts came from a site called bioRxiv.
The ID number of a data set in a public library of data. Ours is GSE186265.
A long code made from a file. If even one letter in the file changes, the code changes. We use it to show a file is unchanged.
A place where scientists run experiments.

left_out: Claim that the proof file passes the project check with no errors: the verifier could not re-run it (not checkable), so we cite only the file and its fingerprint.
The wording '26% of clear-cut orderings reverse overall': the overall share is 29.0% (65,174 of 224,658); 26% is the typical per-pair share, so we use the 29% figure for the whole table.
The claim that the 98 by 15 table is stated by the public data source: it is our own chosen subset, so we describe it as ours.
The claim that published data leave a ceiling versus a true mismatch open: only partly supported and mostly our inference, so we phrase it as 'we do not know'.
The claim that weak promoters are boosted most and that this can reorder enhancers: only partly supported and partly inference, so we do not state it as fact.
Any source or topic excluded by the project's holdout rule.
